tested.summary:
I heard the script once at about 140 words a minute. It has 965 spoken words, about seven and a half minutes counting the three guess holds and the fade. The work folder /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Music/02fc5154-76f5-5aac-a505-860164e7e921/scratchpad/script-rewrite/work-final-newcomers was created and left empty. As told, I opened only round3/viewer-version.md.

Overall, the newcomer version mostly works. All four viewers get the main claim, and all four reason the idle-builders case the right way. Where they get lost:
- the two closing questions;
- the jump from "a whole country" to "one city's homes";
- the vague page 11 line ("partly from that", "building new ones");
- a few idioms that trip the second-language viewer.

These rules held in the spoken text:
- no name for the money view;
- no Klein wording that I could spot;
- numbers written as said;
- no capitals for emphasis and no bracketed cues;
- /məˈteɪi/ is used;
- Mattei's view is said as hers.

THE 15-YEAR-OLD
- Main claim: "New money doesn't always push prices up. If people and machines are doing nothing, it gets more stuff made. If everyone's already busy, prices go up. And the fix for fast-rising prices puts people out of work."
- Terms: inflation, new money, spare, flat-out and interest are fine. The Reserve Bank is "the bank that makes money". They are unsure whether the Reserve Bank is the government. "Loans cost more" means nothing to them until page 12.
- First hesitation: page 1, "the usual cure makes loans cost more". The first real stumble is page 2, "a government like ours can't run out of its own money": is the Reserve Bank the government, and if it can't run out, why can't it pay for everything?
- Examples:
  - Britain is clear: no one spare, fewer things, prices doubled.
  - Glasgow: they follow the story but can't say where the new money comes in, and they notice it's one city, not "a whole country".
  - Japan is clear: the money wasn't spent.
  - New Zealand: they get the guess right but lose "partly from that".
- Case 1 (idle builders): quiet factory, so more homes and prices barely move. That's correct, but page 11's "biggest push came from homes... building new ones" makes them wobble.
- Case 2 (hospitals, builders all busy): flat-out, so prices go up. The direction is right, but they may say "so the hospitals don't get built at all".
- End: "Who pays?" yes: the people who lose their jobs. "Spent on what?" only partly: "what the money buys", and maybe not linked to spare workers.

THE 70-YEAR-OLD WHO LEFT SCHOOL AT 15
- Main claim: "Printing money only pushes prices up when everyone's already working. The way they fight rising prices costs workers their jobs, and this author says that's the point: it keeps wages down."
- Terms: all fine, except they don't believe "can't run out of its own money", which is given with no reason, and they can't say what "like ours" means.
- First hesitation: page 2, that same line.
- Examples:
  - Britain lands well.
  - Glasgow is the most memorable, but they notice it's "one city's homes", not a whole country.
  - Japan: they wonder why the money sat in the banks.
  - New Zealand: they lose "that" on page 11 and may take "building new ones" literally.
- Pages 13 and 15 seem to clash: "They raised rates again and again and prices still went up four point one percent, so the cure didn't work?"
- Case 1: correct.
- Case 2: correct, and they may add that builders and materials get dearer.
- End: "Spent on what?" yes, through Glasgow: money spent where there are no builders. "Who pays?" yes.

THE ADULT WHOSE FIRST LANGUAGE ISN'T ENGLISH
- Main claim: "New money makes prices go up only when no workers or machines are free."
- Terms:
  - "Flat-out" is fine because it's explained.
  - They stumble on "in uniform" (page 6), "homes were already short" (page 7), "set out to" (page 8), "gets more things made" and "aren't any spare" (pages 5 and 16), "partly from that" (page 11), "the year to June" and "if... hadn't changed... would have gone up" (page 15), and "those inside" (page 14).
- First hesitation: page 2's 20-word sentence, "Economists who study how modern money works argue that a government like ours can't run out of its own money". Whose "own money"?
- Examples:
  - Britain is clear from the numbers.
  - Glasgow: they miss the starting point ("short homes"?) but get the rent rise and the refusal to pay.
  - Japan is clear.
  - New Zealand: they get the guess right and are lost on page 11.
- Case 1: correct.
- Case 2: correct direction.
- End: they hear "Spent on what?" literally, as "what is the money used for?", without the spare-workers test. They may hear "who pays?" literally, as "who pays money for the cure?", and only partly recover from the out-of-work dots.

THE BUSY PARENT HALF-WATCHING ON A PHONE
- Main claim: "New money doesn't always raise prices. It depends on whether there are spare workers. Fixing high prices puts people out of work."
- Terms: fine by ear. They miss links that are only on screen: the rule cards tying "spare" to the two factories, and the dots going from 3 to 6 in 100.
- First hesitation: page 3, "Think of each one as a whole country", which is odd without the picture. Then they lose Glasgow's point (81 words, six facts) and page 11's "that".
- Examples: Britain yes. Glasgow comes across as "a rent story". Japan and New Zealand yes.
- Case 1: correct.
- Case 2: correct direction.
- End: "Spent on what?" no; they can only repeat the words. "Who pays?" probably: the people who lose their jobs.

THE TWO CLOSING QUESTIONS
- "Who pays?" works for three of the four, but its answer is never said in one plain sentence.
- "Spent on what?" works reliably for only one or two of the four. Its meaning ("are there spare workers, materials and machines to make what it buys?") is said once, in the middle of page 9, and never tied to the question at the end.

findings.quote: So next time you hear the warning... ask two questions. Spent on what? And who pays for the cure?
findings.problem: "Spent on what?" only works if the viewer remembers page 9's single line, "Are there spare workers, materials and machines to make what it buys?". At the end, page 16 repeats the general rule but never ties the question to it. The second-language viewer hears it literally ("what is the money used for?"). The busy parent can only repeat the words. Only one or two of the four can use it to reason about the hospitals case.
findings.fix: Join the question to the test where it's asked: "Spent on what... and are there spare workers, materials and machines to make it?" On screen, add a small line under SPENT ON WHAT?: ANY SPARE TO MAKE IT?

findings.quote: The biggest push came from homes... building new ones, and rents.
findings.problem: By ear, and on the card BIGGEST PUSH: BUILDING NEW HOMES, AND RENTS over a building site, this can be taken as "building homes pushes prices up". The 70-year-old and the second-language viewer take it literally. That works against the right answer to the idle-builders case, and against the quiet-factory lesson.
findings.fix: Say "the cost of building new ones, and rents", and change the card to COST OF BUILDING NEW HOMES, AND RENTS. Only if the ledger says builders were busy then, add "Builders were busy too" so the flat-out link is plain.

findings.quote: Who pays for the cure?
findings.problem: The question is asked and followed by facts (loans cost more, jobs harder to find, nearly six in a hundred out of work), but the answer is never said in a plain sentence. "Pays" is used in a figurative sense, and the second-language viewer may hear it as "who pays money for the cure?". On page 16 it's also unclear why you'd ask about the cure when you hear a warning about prices.
findings.fix: After "Loans cost more, and jobs got harder to find." add one plain line: "So the people who pay are people with loans... and people who lose their jobs." Keep the hedge "isn't the only reason". On page 16, make the step plain, e.g. "And if they call for the cure... who pays for it?"

findings.quote: Here in New Zealand, the Reserve Bank can.
findings.problem: The page 1 warning says "If the government creates new money". Page 2 says the Reserve Bank creates it, then says "a government like ours can't run out of its own money". Page 3 says new money "is spent" without saying who spends it. Page 10 lists "the Reserve Bank created new money" and "the government spent more" as two separate things. The teen and the second-language viewer ask: is the Reserve Bank the government? Both test cases say "the government pays", so viewers have to guess whether that counts as new money spent.
findings.fix: On page 3, give the spending someone to do it, as a made-up example (no ledger fact needed): "Say the government spends new money on what the factory makes." Only if the ledger supports it, add one clause on page 2 saying how the Reserve Bank and the government are linked.

findings.quote: Economists who study how modern money works argue that a government like ours can't run out of its own money.
findings.problem: This is a 20-word sentence with a 9-word subject before the verb. "Like ours" and "its own money" are never explained. The 70-year-old, who has heard "the country can't afford it" all his life, doesn't believe a claim given with no reason. The second-language viewer can't tell whose money "its own" is.
findings.fix: Split it and say what "like ours" means, as far as the ledger allows: "Some economists study how modern money works. They argue that a government with its own money, like New Zealand's dollar, can't run out of it."

findings.quote: More things get made... and prices barely move.
findings.problem: The film never says why prices barely move. The teen and the busy parent can't explain the quiet-factory half of the rule. Page 6 explains the other half neatly ("More money... and fewer things to buy"), but this half has no matching line.
findings.fix: Use the same pattern as page 6: "More money... and more things to buy. So prices barely move."

findings.quote: Just more money, offered for the same things... and prices go up.
findings.problem: This is the core of the whole film, and it's abstract. "Offered" by whom? It never says who raises the price. The teen asks "but why do prices go up just because there's more money?"
findings.fix: Make it concrete: "People have more money to spend... but there's nothing more to buy. So sellers can ask more... and prices go up."

findings.quote: So for homes, Glasgow was like the flat-out factory.
findings.problem: Page 3 said each factory is "a whole country". Now the factory stands for one city's homes, with no bridge. The 70-year-old and the busy parent notice the jump. Glasgow also never mentions new money or extra spending, so viewers can't say how it supports the rule. Both test cases (builders, hospitals) need this one-kind-of-thing reading.
findings.fix: Add a bridge and a matching line before the tag: "The factory picture works for one kind of thing too. More people needing homes... and hardly any new ones. So for homes, Glasgow was like the flat-out factory."

findings.quote: where homes were already short
findings.problem: "Short" meaning "not enough" is an idiom. The second-language viewer hears "short homes" and misses the starting point of the whole example. The card HOMES ALREADY SHORT repeats it.
findings.fix: Say "where there already weren't enough homes", and change the card to NOT ENOUGH HOMES ALREADY.

findings.quote: Millions were in uniform.
findings.problem: "In uniform", meaning in the armed forces, is an idiom the second-language viewer may not know, and the card MILLIONS IN UNIFORM doesn't help. Viewers also aren't told why it matters: workers left their jobs.
findings.fix: Say "Millions went off to fight." and change the card to MILLIONS WENT TO FIGHT. The next line (fewer than one in a hundred out of work) then makes the link.

findings.quote: partly from that, and partly from world prices, like oil.
findings.problem: "That" points vaguely back to "almost no one was waiting at the gate". By ear, the second-language viewer, the busy parent and the 70-year-old lose it. After Japan ("it's whether it's spent"), viewers also want to know whether money was being spent this time, but page 10 lists the Reserve Bank and government spending as two separate facts. The card PARTLY: FEW SPARE is clearer than the speech.
findings.fix: Match the card and use page 10's own fact: "partly because more was being spent while almost no one was spare, and partly from world prices, like oil."

findings.quote: In the year to June twenty twenty-six, prices here went up four point one percent. If petrol and diesel prices hadn't changed... prices would have gone up two point nine percent.
findings.problem: "The year to June" is office language. "If... hadn't changed... would have gone up" is hard for the second-language viewer. There is also an accuracy question: a figure that leaves petrol and diesel out is not the same as one where they hadn't changed (the two differ slightly). If the ledger's entry is a "leave them out" figure, both the speech and the card say something stronger than the ledger. I could not check this.
findings.fix: Check the ledger wording. If it's a "leave them out" figure, say: "In the twelve months to June twenty twenty-six, prices here went up four point one percent. Leave out petrol and diesel... and prices went up two point nine percent." Change the card to match.

findings.quote: From late twenty twenty-one into twenty twenty-three, the Reserve Bank raised its interest rate again and again.
findings.problem: Page 12 says the cure makes prices go up more slowly. Page 13 shows the cure used again and again. Page 15 then shows prices up four point one percent in the year to mid twenty twenty-six. The 70-year-old concludes either "the cure didn't work" or "the film contradicts itself". The film never says what happened to prices after the cure, or that fuel is outside what the cure can reach.
findings.fix: On page 15, after the fuel line, add a short bridge in plain words, as far as the ledger and rules allow, e.g. "The cure works on spending here... it can't make world fuel cheaper." Or say what happened to prices after the rate rises, if the ledger has it.

findings.quote: She argues that putting people out of work is the main goal.
findings.problem: It isn't said whose goal, or the goal of what. Right after "our Reserve Bank... see putting people out of work as unfortunate", it can be heard as "the Reserve Bank secretly wants us unemployed". That may be stronger than, or different from, Mattei's claim in the ledger. I could not check this.
findings.fix: Anchor it to the cure, using the ledger's wording: "She argues that putting people out of work is the cure's main goal." Check the ledger entry for how strong her claim is.

findings.quote: With more workers waiting at the gate, she says, those inside have less power to ask for more pay.
findings.problem: "Those inside" stretches the picture further; the second-language viewer may not read it as "people with jobs". The film says who pays, but never names who gains (the Klein-spirit rule: who gains and who pays). The 70-year-old works it out; the others don't.
findings.fix: Say "those still in work have less power to ask for more pay." Only if the ledger has it, name who gains as her view, e.g. "That suits employers, she argues."

findings.quote: the usual cure makes loans cost more
findings.problem: The teen has no loans, and how a loan "costs more" isn't explained until page 12, about five minutes later. This is a small early stumble in the hook.
findings.fix: Give a familiar example: "the usual cure makes loans, like home loans, cost more."

findings.quote: new money, once it's spent, mostly gets more things made. When there aren't any spare... it mostly pushes prices up.
findings.problem: "Gets more things made" and the shortened "aren't any spare" are hard for the second-language viewer. By ear, the rule uses "spare" while the pictures were named "the quiet factory" and "the flat-out factory". Only the screen links them, so the busy parent misses it. "The quiet factory" is never named again after page 3. The same wording comes back on page 16.
findings.fix: On pages 5 and 16: "When there are spare workers, materials and machines, like the quiet factory... new money, once it's spent, mostly means more things are made. When nothing is spare, like the flat-out factory... it mostly pushes prices up."

findings.quote: No spare workers, materials or machines... so no more things get made.
findings.problem: For the hospitals case, a literal viewer (the teen) concludes "the hospitals won't get built at all". Glasgow already shows the real swap (builders went to the war, so homes weren't built), but the film never says it in so many words.
findings.fix: On page 7, make the swap plain: "Builders busy with the war... weren't building homes." That gives viewers what they need for "build hospitals and something else doesn't get built, and prices go up".

findings.quote: Japan's version of our Reserve Bank set out to double the money it had created... in two years.
findings.problem: "Set out to" is a phrasal verb that's hard for the second-language viewer. "The money it had created" can be heard as "all the money in Japan".
findings.fix: "Japan's version of our Reserve Bank planned to double, in two years, the money it had created." Check the ledger for exactly what was to double.

findings.quote: most of the new money just sat in the banks
findings.problem: The teen and the 70-year-old wonder which banks, and why the money would just sit there. The next line ("never reached the factory") helps, but "spent" isn't said here.
findings.fix: Add three words: "most of the new money just sat in the banks... it wasn't spent."

findings.quote: The Reserve Bank raises its interest rate. Interest is the extra you pay back when you borrow. Many loans cost more
findings.problem: "Interest" is explained but "rate" isn't. It's never said how the Reserve Bank's own rate makes your loan cost more. The teen and the second-language viewer miss the step.
findings.fix: If the ledger has it: "The Reserve Bank raises its interest rate... and banks charge more on loans, like home loans."

findings.quote: nearly six in a hundred were out of work
findings.problem: To see the rise, viewers have to remember page 10's "three in a hundred". The busy parent only gets the comparison from the returning dot panel, which they may not be watching.
findings.fix: "nearly six in a hundred were out of work... up from about three."

findings.quote: So part of what you felt at the checkout wasn't new money being spent.
findings.problem: This can be heard as "and the rest was new money being spent", which the film doesn't claim and the ledger may not support.
findings.fix: Name the cause instead: "So part of what you felt at the checkout came from world fuel prices... not from new money being spent here."

findings.quote: Our Reserve Bank, and others like it, see putting people out of work as unfortunate... but not the goal.
findings.problem: No ledger entry gives our Reserve Bank's view on this. The only support is one line in C2-M17's 'simplified or contested' column: "Central banks frame job losses as an 'unfortunate cost', not a goal". No source is named for that line. C2-M17's own sources are America's central bank (Powell, 2022) and Australia's. The ledger lists the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's pages as blocked (403). I opened Powell's speech, which the ledger cites, and the words are his: "These are the unfortunate costs of reducing inflation." He also talks of "softer labor market conditions" and "some pain", which is milder than "putting people out of work". So the line puts a sourced American view into our Reserve Bank's mouth. The screen card OUR RESERVE BANK AND OTHERS LIKE IT: UNFORTUNATE, NOT THE GOAL has the same problem.
findings.fix: Either (a) before recording, open a Reserve Bank of New Zealand source that says this and add it to the ledger, or (b) name the bank the ledger does support, using C2-M17's plain wording: "America's version of our Reserve Bank has said its cure brings some pain, including fewer jobs... an unfortunate cost, but not the goal." Change the card to match, and ask the ledger's owner to add Powell's 'unfortunate costs' sentence to C2-M17's claim column.

findings.quote: She argues that putting people out of work is the main goal.
findings.problem: This is stronger than C2-H18's own words. Mattei (The Nation, 2023) says: "The main objective of interest rate hikes is to cool down the labor market" and "Fewer job openings and higher unemployment diminish the bargaining power of workers". In RevDem she calls unemployment "the best disciplinary device to suppress wages". So her main objective is a cooler job market, meaning fewer openings as well as more people out of work. In her account, unemployment is the tool used to weaken workers. The ledger's plain version describes it as the means ("works by putting people out of work"), and the second fact check only confirmed "part of the point". The new line leaves out the fewer-openings half and turns her means into the goal. The card MATTEI ARGUES: THE MAIN GOAL goes with it.
findings.fix: "She argues that the main goal is fewer jobs, and more people out of work." Keep the next sentence ("With more workers waiting at the gate, she says...") as it is. This pairs with the fix above ("including fewer jobs... not the goal"), so the two views still clash out loud. Card: MATTEI ARGUES: THE MAIN GOAL: FEWER JOBS.

findings.quote: The biggest push came from homes... building new ones, and rents.
findings.problem: To answer the question: Stats NZ's 'driven mainly by' is about one group, not the whole 7.3%. The release the ledger cites (republished Stats NZ text, opened today) says: "The main driver for the 7.3 percent annual inflation to the June 2022 quarter was the housing and household utilities group, due to rising prices for construction and rentals for housing", and "The next largest contributor to annual inflation was from the transport group, due to higher prices for petrol and diesel." So 'the biggest push' is correct, but there are two problems. (1) It holds only for the year to June 2022, while the page is talking about the whole price rise. (2) 'homes... building new ones' can be heard as house prices, or as the building work itself. The item that rose is the price of building a new home, and house prices are not in the figure (ledger Trap, C2-N08). The research note also puts the ledger's paraphrase in quotation marks as if it were Stats NZ's words.
findings.fix: "At the peak, the biggest push came from the cost of building new homes... and from rents." Fix the note so it quotes Stats NZ's real sentence. Tell the ledger's owner that C2-N02's claim column should say the housing group was the main driver, with transport (petrol and diesel) next.

findings.quote: So part of what you felt at the checkout wasn't new money being spent.
findings.problem: This conclusion only holds if the 2026 fuel rise came from outside New Zealand's spending, and the ledger hasn't checked that. C2-N05 says "Cause of the 2026 fuel spike not researched in this lane". The New Zealand 'Could not verify (kept out of the film)' list includes "Cause of the 2026 fuel price spike". The only support is C2-M04's note that Westpac blames the Middle East war, and C2-M04 was read from search results. The Trap says to open the page before a medium entry goes in.
findings.fix: Before recording, open one source on why petrol and diesel went up in the year to June 2026 (Westpac's or Stats NZ's release) and add it to the ledger. If it can't be sourced, the line can't say what the fuel rise wasn't caused by.

findings.quote: In the year to June twenty twenty-six, prices here went up four point one percent. If petrol and diesel prices hadn't changed... prices would have gone up two point nine percent.
findings.problem: These figures go out of date soon. The September quarter figures come out on 22 October 2026, and C2-XC05 says they replace these. The June-year wording stays true, but it won't be the latest figure. Page 1's present-tense "costs more than it did a year ago" also rests on whatever the latest figure is.
findings.fix: If the film comes out after 22 October, put the September figures into the ledger first, then decide whether to switch. Keep the dated June wording if you don't switch, and never say 'mostly fuel'.

findings.quote: By the middle of twenty twenty-six... nearly six in a hundred were out of work.
findings.problem: This figure goes out of date soon. C2-XD05 gives 5.6% for the June 2026 quarter, and the next release is 4 November 2026. The series gets revised (March was revised to 5.4%), so the June figure itself could change.
findings.fix: After 4 November, check that the June quarter still reads about 5.6%. If it is revised to 5.4% or below, 'nearly six' no longer fits, so say 'more than five in a hundred'. The 28 October Reserve Bank decision doesn't touch any line.

findings.quote: With builders and materials gone to the war, few new homes were built.
findings.problem: This sentence names a cause, and its support is thin. It rests on a second fact check row that has no id. That row's evidence that 'house building virtually ceased' is Merrett and Sykes quoted second-hand from a search result. 'Labour and materials were diverted to the war' is the checker's own line with no source, and it is about Britain generally, not Glasgow. It is probably true, but it is the weakest link on the page.
findings.fix: Open a source before recording (Merrett and Sykes, or another Glasgow or British housing history) and give it an id. Otherwise say less: "And with the war on, few new homes were built."

findings.quote: It also tries to stop prices going up too fast.
findings.problem: Verdict: supported, and no stronger than the ledger. C2-N04 and C2-M04 give the Reserve Bank's 1-3% target band, C2-M15 dates New Zealand's inflation targeting to about 1990, and C2-M17 says central banks fight inflation by raising interest rates. Two small points. The notes don't cite C2-M17, which is the most direct support. And the target is a band, so the Bank also acts when prices go up too slowly. That is what Japan's version was doing on page 8 (it aimed for 2%, C2-C06 and C2-XB03), and the listener is never told.
findings.fix: Add C2-M17 to page 2's ids. No change to the narration is needed. If page 8 tests as confusing, the optional 'It even wanted prices to go up' line is supported by C2-C06.

findings.quote: partly from that, and partly from world prices, like oil.
findings.problem: Verdict: supported, and kept within the entries. C2-N16 says no published split exists, with evidence on both sides; its plain version says "Part came from the world: oil, shipping, war. Part came from here." C2-N03 gives tradables at 8.2% and non-tradables at 6.6%. The best support is C2-N14 (the Royal Commission: the economic response 'in part' contributed to cost-of-living pressures, with international forces also significant), and the notes don't cite it. C2-N16 is medium confidence, and C2-N02 says the world-oil link was 'not researched here in detail'.
findings.fix: Add C2-N14 to page 11's ids. Note that C2-N16 is medium confidence and was not read from the full page. No change to the narration.

findings.quote: the usual cure makes loans cost more
findings.problem: This drops a qualification. C2-XD01 says "higher charges on many mortgages and loans". Page 12 keeps 'Many loans cost more', but page 1 and page 13 ("Loans cost more, and jobs got harder to find.") drop 'many'.
findings.fix: Page 1: "the usual cure makes many loans cost more". Page 13: "Many loans cost more, and jobs got harder to find."

findings.quote: And prices go up more slowly. Not down... just more slowly.
findings.problem: 'Not down' is stated as a rule, but C2-XD01 only says prices go up less quickly. The ledger also shows prices falling about a fifth after Britain's 1920 rate rise (C2-H09). That case is cut from this chapter but belongs to the series.
findings.fix: "Usually not down... just more slowly."

findings.quote: the almost-level line ABOUT ½% A YEAR
findings.problem: The second fact check's final reviewer advised putting 'UNDER 1% A YEAR' or 'ABOUT 0.6% A YEAR' on screen, because the 2013-2021 average is about 0.6% (C2-XB04). The spoken 'about half a percent' was judged fair, and the card follows Malina's words, so this is a small point.
findings.fix: Keep the narration. Either keep the card as a short form of what Malina says, or follow the reviewer's choice: UNDER 1% A YEAR.

tested.summary: I checked every factual sentence on all 16 pages against its ledger entry, the second fact check of 12 October (and its JSON) and the Traps. The narration file matches the script word for word. Most lines hold up: Britain, Glasgow's numbers, Japan, New Zealand 2020-21, the dates of the rate rises, 4.1% and 2.9% (Stats NZ's own wording), and every 'partly', 'about', 'one reason' and 'isn't the only reason' is kept. Answers to the lines no one else has checked: (1) Page 2, "It also tries to stop prices going up too fast", is supported by C2-N04, C2-M04, C2-M15 and C2-M17. No change needed; just add C2-M17 to the ids. (2) Page 11, "partly from that, and partly from world prices", is supported by C2-N16, C2-N03 and C2-N14; add C2-N14 to the ids. (3) Page 11's homes line: I opened the Stats NZ release the ledger cites. "Driven mainly by" describes only the housing and household utilities group, which was the main driver of the 7.3%, with transport (petrol and diesel) next. So "the biggest push" is right, but only for the year to June 2022, and "homes... building new ones" should say "the cost of building new homes" so nobody hears house prices. The ledger's own paraphrase in C2-N02 overstates Stats NZ slightly. (4) Page 14's bank line is a must-fix. The ledger has no source for our Reserve Bank's view. "Unfortunate costs" is Powell's phrase from America's central bank (I confirmed it in his 2022 speech), and the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's pages were blocked. (5) Page 14's Mattei line is a must-fix. C2-H18's own words make "cool down the labor market" (fewer job openings and higher unemployment) the main objective, with unemployment as the tool against workers. "Putting people out of work is the main goal" is stronger than that, and also stronger than the checked "part of the point". The suggested fixes ("fewer jobs" on both sides) keep the clash audible. Page 15's "wasn't new money being spent" depends on the cause of the 2026 fuel rise, which the ledger lists as not checked. findings.quote: Our Reserve Bank, and others like it, see putting people out of work as unfortunate... but not the goal.

Verdict: the new script mostly fixes both complaints. Nothing left would lose a newcomer outright, so nothing is marked must-fix. What's left is a short fast stretch in the middle, a few lines a newcomer could misread, and an ending that goes flat.

Too fast: fixed for most pages. I tagged every page by hand using the same kinds of item as the first-round audit: places, years, numbers and terms.
- Overall load fell from 4.0 items every 10 seconds in the recorded film to about 2.
- Places, years and numbers fell from 52 to 29.
- The busiest page fell from 5.7 items every 10 seconds to 4.0.
- Pages 1, 3, 4, 5, 11, 12, 14 and 16 are calm, at 0.5 to 1.6 items every 10 seconds.
- The stretch that is still fast is Britain, then Glasgow, then Japan (pages 6 to 8): about 80 seconds carrying 26 items.
  - Glasgow (page 7) carries the most: 11 items in 82 words.
  - Japan's set-up (page 8) is as dense per second as the old film's average.
- Page 2 is the heaviest page of the opening, with four ideas in about 20 seconds before any picture.
- The script alone can't fix pace. Malina ran at 164 words a minute, and a "..." gives less than a second. At that speed the film is about 6:55; at 150 a minute it's about 7:25.

Words people don't know: largely fixed. Every hard word in the recording is gone or explained ("unemployment", "central bank", "yen", "shares", "the 2008 crash", "heartland", "marks", "dearer"). Weak spots remain, but none blocks understanding:
- "in uniform" and "homes were already short" (idioms)
- "sat in the banks"
- "help with wages"
- "world prices" (explained four pages later)
- "building new ones" (easily misheard)
- who creates money: page 1 says the government, page 2 says the Reserve Bank, and nothing says how the two are linked
- the only numbers without a plain anchor: four point one and two point nine percent on page 15

Gone too far the other way? The script isn't padded or patronising line by line. Three "Have a guess" prompts and the one-line definition of interest suit a mixed audience. Line trims save only 15 to 30 words. The real length risk is structural:
- Pages 12 to 16 run about 2 minutes 20 seconds after the last guess, with nothing for the viewer to do.
- Page 15 turns to fuel sums right after Mattei's view, which is the high point.
- If 7 minutes is too long for a phone, cut or fold page 15, or split the film between pages 11 and 12. Trimming lines won't get there.
- My fixes as written add about 25 words.

Urgency in the spirit of Naomi Klein:
- The opening has stakes, direct questions and the viewer's own experience.
- It goes flat on page 13, where the "who pays" page ends on a hedge and gives people only as "nearly six in a hundred" with nothing to compare it to.
- It goes flat again on page 15 (sums).
- The cure section names who pays but never who gains.
- The script dropped the live stake: the Reserve Bank has started raising its rate again this year.

findings.problem: This is the longest and heaviest page: 82 words, about 31 to 33 seconds, 11 items (two dates, two numbers, a new place, Parliament). 'So for homes, Glasgow was like the flat-out factory' quietly changes what the picture stands for, from 'a whole country' to homes in one city. The line doesn't name either half of the match, so many newcomers won't hear Glasgow as the first 'on what' case that the closing 'Spent on what?' depends on.
findings.fix: 'By nineteen fifteen, crowds of war workers had come to Glasgow. Homes there were already short. With builders and materials gone to the war, few new homes were built. So for homes, Glasgow was like the flat-out factory. More people needed somewhere to live... and there was hardly anyone spare to build.' findings.quote: And prices here went up fast... partly from that, and partly from world prices, like oil. The biggest push came from homes... building new ones, and rents.

findings.fix: 'And prices here went up fast... partly from that, and partly from world prices, like fuel. The biggest push came from homes. Building new ones cost more... and rents went up.' Here 'cost more' keeps the script's one meaning: the price went up.

findings.quote: Economists who study how modern money works argue that a government like ours can't run out of its own money. But it can run out of workers, materials and machines.
findings.problem: Before any picture, the newcomer gets the Reserve Bank's two jobs, a new group of economists, the series' most surprising claim and the real limit, all in about 20 seconds. That is 2.8 to 3.1 items every 10 seconds, the heaviest page of the opening, and the chapter never comes back to the claim. Who creates money also shifts: page 1 says 'If the government creates new money', page 2 says 'the Reserve Bank can', and then 'a government like ours can't run out of its own money'. Nothing says how the two are linked, so a newcomer can't tell whose money it is.
findings.fix: (1) On page 1, take the actor out of the warning: 'If new money is created... prices will go up.' Page 2's 'Who can create new money?' then becomes the natural next question. (2) Move these two sentences, word for word, to the end of page 5, after the rule. There 'run out of workers, materials and machines' already has a picture behind it, which puts the concrete before the idea as the Pinker toolkit asks. Page 2 then ends on 'It also tries to stop prices going up too fast.' If they stay on page 2, do (1) at least. Saying how the Reserve Bank and the government are linked would need a ledger entry first.

findings.quote: So when there are spare workers, materials and machines... new money, once it's spent, mostly gets more things made.
findings.problem: The film's key sentence, said again word for word on page 16, has an aside between its subject and verb. The rules file's newcomer section says never to do that. It also gives the two conditions in the opposite order to page 9's recap ('whether it's spent... and on what').
findings.fix: Use the same words on both pages: 'So when new money is spent... and there are spare workers, materials and machines... it mostly gets more things made. When there aren't any spare... it mostly pushes prices up.' This keeps the 'spent' condition the fact tester asked for (C2-XA03) and matches page 9's order. Update the Traps line to 'keep when new money is spent'.

findings.quote: From late twenty twenty-one into twenty twenty-three, the Reserve Bank raised its interest rate again and again.
findings.problem: There are three dates in two sentences. The 'who pays' page gives people only as 'nearly six in a hundred', with nothing to compare it to ('three in a hundred' came about 75 seconds earlier). The page ends on the hedge 'The interest rate isn't the only reason for that'. So the urgency goes flat at the very moment the film asks who pays. By the middle of twenty twenty-six... nearly six in a hundred were out of work. Up from about three. The interest rate isn't the only reason for that. And this year, the Reserve Bank has started raising its interest rate again.' Sources: C2-N10, and C2-N11 for the from-to pair. For the last line, C2-XD04 asks for exactly this tense. findings.fix: In the edit, hold about 2 seconds of picture and music after page 5 (rule cards on screen) and after page 9 (recap card). Listen to whether Malina speeds up on the short sentences. Plan the length at about 164 a minute, as the rules file says (about 6:55 in all), not at 140 (7:55).

fixed.how_it_teaches:
The sentence a viewer should be able to say back: whether new money pushes prices up depends on whether it's spent, and on what. When new money is spent and there are spare workers, materials and machines to make what it buys, it mostly gets more things made. When nothing is spare, it mostly pushes prices up. And the usual cure is paid for by many people with loans and by people put out of work.

How the film gets there:
- One made-up picture comes before any real case: two factories, each standing for "a whole country... all its workers, materials and machines".
  - The quiet factory: the government spends new money on what it makes. "More money... and more things to buy. So prices barely move."
  - The flat-out factory: "More money... for the same things. So sellers can ask more... and prices go up."
  - Page 6 completes the pattern with Britain: more, the same, then fewer things to buy.
- The rule is said in the same words on pages 5 and 16: "When new money is spent... and there are spare workers, materials and machines... it mostly gets more things made. When nothing is spare... it mostly pushes prices up."
- Each real case is placed on the picture out loud:
  - Britain at war is "close to the flat-out factory".
  - Glasgow: "Our picture works for one kind of thing too. For homes, Glasgow was like the flat-out factory." It shows the swap: builders gone to the war, so few new homes.
  - Japan's money "never reached the factory", then the recap: "whether it's spent... and on what. Are there spare workers, materials and machines to make what it buys?"
  - New Zealand 2020-21 is the application check: clue, guess, answer. Prices went up partly because more was being spent with almost no one at the gate, and partly because of prices overseas. At the peak, the biggest push came from the price of building new homes, and rents.
- The cure is placed on the picture: the flat-out factory slows, and more workers wait at the gate.
- Who pays is asked and then answered plainly ("Many people with loans... and people put out of work"), with the out-of-work share compared in one unit (about three, then nearly six in a hundred).
- The two views clash on the same two words, "fewer jobs": America's version of our Reserve Bank calls them unfortunate, not the goal; Mattei argues they are the cure's main goal.
- The checkout returns in the page 1 basket's own unit, dollars: a hundred, about a hundred and four, about a hundred and three if petrol and diesel prices hadn't changed. Petrol and diesel push prices up in both factories.
- The close joins the question to its test: "Spent on what... and is anything spare to make it? And who pays for the cure?"

Supports for the viewer:
- three guesses, each held 4 seconds;
- 2-second picture holds after the rule (page 5) and the Japan recap (page 9);
- every term explained at first use, with one plain name per thing;
- Mattei's view marked "she argues" and "she says";
- the money view never named;
- Klein's spirit only: stakes first, direct questions, who gains and who pays.

You've heard the warning too. If new money is created... prices will go up. Is that always true? It matters... because when prices go up too fast, the usual cure makes many loans cost more. pages.name: Who can create new money
pages.text: Who can create new money? Here in New Zealand, the Reserve Bank can. It also tries to stop prices going up too fast. There are economists who study how modern money works. They argue that our government can't run out of its own money. But it can run out of workers, materials and machines.

last.how_it_teaches:
The sentence a viewer should be able to say back: whether new money pushes prices up depends on whether it's spent, and on what. When new money is spent and there are spare workers, materials and machines to make what it buys, it mostly gets more things made. When nothing is spare, it mostly pushes prices up. And the usual cure is paid for by many people with loans and by people put out of work.

The model comes first: two factories, each standing for "a whole country... all its workers, materials and machines". The quiet factory (workers wait at the gate): "More money... and more things to buy. So prices barely move." The flat-out factory (everyone working as hard as they can): "More money... for the same things. So sellers can ask more... and prices go up." Money that is never spent never reaches the factory. The rule is said in the same words on pages 5 and 16.

Then the real cases, in time order, each placed on the picture out loud: Britain at war ("close to the flat-out factory"; "More money... and fewer things to buy"); Glasgow's homes ("Our picture works for one kind of thing too. For homes, Glasgow was like the flat-out factory"); Japan (most of the new money "never reached the factory", then the recap "whether it's spent... and on what. Are there spare workers, materials and machines to make what it buys?"); New Zealand 2020-21 as the test (clue, guess, then "Close to the flat-out factory", prices up "partly because more was being spent... and partly because of prices overseas, like oil"); the usual cure placed on the picture; who pays, answered plainly ("Many people with loans... and people put out of work"); two views clashing on the same words (America's version of our Reserve Bank: fewer jobs are "unfortunate... but not the goal"; Mattei "argues that fewer jobs are the cure's main goal"); and back at the checkout, a hundred-dollar basket that became about a hundred and four, about a hundred and three without the petrol and diesel change.

Checks for the viewer: three guesses at page ends, each held about 4 seconds (the flat-out factory, Japan, New Zealand). Recaps in the same words: the rule twice (pages 5 and 16); "whether it's spent... and on what" after Japan; "Who pays for the cure?" asked and answered on page 13 and asked again at the end; and the closing "Spent on what... and is anything spare to make what it buys?", which now ends in page 9's exact words, so "it" keeps meaning new money all through page 16.

Naomi Klein in spirit only: stakes in the first 30 seconds, the viewer's own questions asked and answered, who gains and who pays side by side, people counted as people, urgency from facts. Pinker's principles, not his voice: a concrete scene before each idea, the imagined picture announced as imagined, where the picture changes what it stands for said aloud, qualifications kept ("mostly", "close to", "partly", "many", "usually", "probably"). Full notes, ready cuts, traps and the listener questions are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Music/02fc5154-76f5-5aac-a505-860164e7e921/scratchpad/script-rewrite/work-final-last/final.md; the narration alone is /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-Music/02fc5154-76f5-5aac-a505-860164e7e921/scratchpad/script-rewrite/work-final-last/narration-final.txt.

pages.name: The question
pages.text: You've felt it at the checkout. The same basket of shopping costs more than it did a year ago. That's inflation... prices in general, going up. The whole basket. You've heard the warning too. If new money is created... prices will go up. Is that always true? It matters... because when prices go up too fast, the usual cure makes many loans cost more. And that can put people out of work.
terms_explained: inflation ("prices in general, going up... the whole basket"); the usual cure (it "makes many loans cost more"; in full on page 12).
pages.pictures: as before (page-1 reused, parts swapped, code only). The politician still mouths the warning: NEW MONEY → PRICES UP?, then IS THAT ALWAYS TRUE?, then MANY LOANS COST MORE → OUT OF WORK. The one-tag-swings beat is shortened to match the cut line: every tag flips: THE WHOLE BASKET.

pages.name: Who can create new money
pages.text: Who can create new money? Here in New Zealand, the Reserve Bank can. It also tries to stop prices going up too fast. There are economists who study how modern money works. They argue that our government can't run out of its own money. But it can run out of workers, materials and machines.
terms_explained: who can create new money; the Reserve Bank and what it tries to do; the economists' view, in its own sentence and marked "argue"; workers, materials and machines as the real limit.
pages.pictures: (code only): page-10's New Zealand street at dusk with the typed card THE RESERVE BANK (no logo) and a small CAN CREATE NEW MONEY; then TRIES TO STOP PRICES GOING UP TOO FAST; page-2's banknote bundles land: NEW MONEY; the card CAN'T RUN OUT OF ITS OWN MONEY / CAN RUN OUT OF..., then page-3's three cut-outs pop up: WORKERS / MATERIALS / MACHINES.

pages.name: The quiet factory
pages.text: Picture two factories. Think of each one as a whole country... all its workers, materials and machines. In the first, the machines stand still. Workers wait at the gate, hoping for a job. Call it the quiet factory. Now the government spends new money on what the factory makes. The workers go in. The machines start. More money... and more things to buy. So prices barely move.
terms_explained: the two-factories picture and what it stands for; the quiet factory; who spends the new money in the picture; why prices barely move (more money, and more things to buy).
pages.pictures: page-3's works A; A WHOLE COUNTRY: WORKERS, MATERIALS, MACHINES; THE QUIET FACTORY; coins rain in: THE GOVERNMENT SPENDS NEW MONEY; the workers go in and goods come out: MORE MONEY / MORE THINGS TO BUY (the same layout page 6 uses for MORE MONEY / FEWER THINGS); the price counter stays put.

pages.name: The flat-out factory, the first guess
pages.text: In the second factory, every worker and every machine is already busy... working as hard as they can. No one waits at the gate. Call it the flat-out factory. The same new money is spent on what this factory makes. What happens to prices? Have a guess.
terms_explained: flat out; the flat-out factory. The guess now names what to guess about.
pages.pictures: page-3's works B, gate empty, labelled THE FLAT-OUT FACTORY with a small line under it: FLAT OUT = WORKING AS HARD AS THEY CAN. Coins rain in; the counter freezes. WHAT HAPPENS TO PRICES? held about 4 seconds, with a small on-screen marker that the film is waiting for a guess.

pages.name: The rule
pages.text: No spare workers, materials or machines... so no extra things get made. More money... for the same things. So sellers can ask more... and prices go up. Most economists agree on this much. When new money is spent... and there are spare workers, materials and machines... it mostly gets more things made. When nothing is spare... it mostly pushes prices up.
terms_explained: spare; why prices go up (sellers can ask more); the rule (recap 1, repeated word for word on page 16), now with "spent" first, in the same order as page 9's "whether it's spent... and on what".
pages.pictures: works B's counter flips up; the three cut-outs return stamped NO SPARE, with MORE MONEY / SAME THINGS, then SELLERS CAN ASK MORE, and a small MOST ECONOMISTS AGREE. Then the wide shot of both works with two rule cards: NEW MONEY SPENT + SPARE → MOSTLY MORE THINGS MADE and NOTHING SPARE → MOSTLY PRICES UP. Hold the rule cards about 2 seconds after Malina stops, with the music up, before the page turn.

pages.name: Britain at war
pages.text: Now a real case. Britain, during the First World War. Millions went to fight. Soon, fewer than one worker in a hundred was out of work. German submarines sank ships carrying food and materials. And the war was paid for partly with new money. More money... and fewer things to buy. By the end of the war, prices had roughly doubled. Britain at war was close to the flat-out factory.
terms_explained: out of work (one worker in a hundred); why workers weren't spare (millions went to fight).
pages.pictures: page-2's munitions hall, words matched (code only): BRITAIN, FIRST WORLD WAR; a typed card MILLIONS WENT TO FIGHT; the 100 dots, last nearly empty: FEWER THAN 1 IN 100 OUT OF WORK; SHIPS SUNK: FOOD, MATERIALS; PARTLY NEW MONEY; MORE MONEY / FEWER THINGS; bars 1914 ×1 and 1918 ABOUT ×2; quick cut to works B: CLOSE TO THE FLAT-OUT FACTORY.

pages.name: Glasgow's homes
pages.text: By nineteen fifteen, crowds of war workers had come to Glasgow. There were already too few homes. With builders and materials gone to the war, few new ones were built. Our picture works for one kind of thing too. For homes, Glasgow was like the flat-out factory. Landlords raised the rent... in places by up to a quarter. By November, about twenty thousand families were refusing to pay the extra. Within weeks, Britain's Parliament brought rents on small homes back to what they were before the war.
terms_explained: too few homes (plain words in place of "homes were already short"); the picture standing for one kind of thing, said aloud before it is used; the swap (builders busy with the war, so few new homes); Britain's Parliament.
pages.pictures: page-4's Glasgow tenement street (code only), titled GLASGOW 1915, with TOO FEW HOMES ALREADY; workers stream in; the building-site shot: BUILDERS AND MATERIALS GONE TO WAR / FEW NEW HOMES; a quick wide shot of works B shrinking to a row of tenements, with the small card ONE KIND OF THING; the tag FOR HOMES: LIKE THE FLAT-OUT FACTORY; RENT RAISED / UP TO +25% IN PLACES; the counter to 20,000 FAMILIES REFUSING THE EXTRA; the stamp RENTS BACK TO BEFORE THE WAR. Never WON or RENTS FROZEN. No Mary Barbour card. Never "NOT ENOUGH HOMES" (a Naomi Klein title).

pages.name: Japan, the second guess
pages.text: Japan, twenty thirteen. Japan's version of our Reserve Bank planned to double the money it had created... in two years. If the warning is right, prices should go up fast. What do you think happened? Have a guess.
terms_explained: Japan's version of our Reserve Bank (meaningful, since page 2 said what ours does). "Planned to" replaces "set out to".
pages.pictures: unchanged (page-5 part A, JAPAN 2013, ×2 MONEY / IN TWO YEARS, the dashed line IF THE WARNING IS RIGHT climbs under WHAT HAPPENED?), hold about 4 seconds.

pages.name: Japan, the answer
pages.text: Prices barely moved... for about eight years. On average, they went up about half a percent a year. Why? One reason economists give... most of the new money just sat in the banks. In our picture, most of it never reached the factory. So it's not just how much new money there is. It's whether it's spent... and on what. Are there spare workers, materials and machines to make what it buys?
terms_explained: money created but not spent; recap 2, and what "on what" asks. The two numbers are now in separate sentences.
pages.pictures: as before (the almost-level line ABOUT ½% A YEAR; coins piling up in front of the card bank: MOST SAT IN THE BANKS; NOT JUST HOW MUCH / WHETHER IT'S SPENT, AND ON WHAT), then the typed card SPARE WORKERS, MATERIALS, MACHINES TO MAKE WHAT IT BUYS? Hold that card about 2 seconds after Malina stops, before the page turn.

pages.name: New Zealand, the third guess
pages.text: Now, here. When Covid hit in twenty twenty, the Reserve Bank created new money. And the government spent more... including help paying wages. By the end of twenty twenty-one, almost everyone looking for work had found it. Only about three in a hundred were out of work. Which factory was New Zealand closer to? Have a guess.
terms_explained: out of work as a share ("about three in a hundred"); what part of the government's money went on (paying wages); "almost everyone looking for work had found it".
pages.pictures: page-8 part B's New Zealand street (code only): NEW ZEALAND 2020; notes land: NEW MONEY; GOVERNMENT SPENT MORE / INCLUDING HELP PAYING WAGES; 2021 with the 100-dot panel, 3 empty: ABOUT 3 IN 100 OUT OF WORK, credited Stats NZ (the LOWEST IN 30+ YEARS card is removed with its line); wide shot of both factories: WHICH ONE?, held about 4 seconds.

pages.name: New Zealand, the answer
pages.text: Close to the flat-out factory. Almost no one was waiting at the gate. And prices here went up fast. Partly because more was being spent... and partly because of prices overseas, like oil. At the peak, the biggest push came from the price of building new homes... and rents.
terms_explained: none new. It says the outcome and gives both causes in plain words: "more was being spent" (the page 10 spending, with almost no one spare) and "prices overseas". "At the peak" ties the homes line to the year prices went up fastest.
pages.pictures: (code only, no new paintings): quick cut to works B with the gate almost empty: CLOSE TO THE FLAT-OUT FACTORY. Then PRICES WENT UP FAST, splitting into two small cards: PARTLY: MORE SPENT and PARTLY: PRICES OVERSEAS, LIKE OIL (page-7 part A's oil barrel, no counter). Then page-4's building-site shot relabelled NEW ZEALAND with AT THE PEAK: THE PRICE OF BUILDING NEW HOMES, AND RENTS. Never BUILDING NEW HOMES on its own. No house-price figures, no +30%, no review desk.

pages.name: The usual cure
pages.text: So what's the usual cure? The Reserve Bank raises its interest rate. Interest is the extra you pay back when you borrow. Many loans cost more... so people have less to spend. Businesses sell fewer things, and hire fewer people. And prices go up more slowly. Usually not down... just more slowly. In our picture, the flat-out factory slows... and more workers wait at the gate.
terms_explained: interest and interest rate; the usual cure in full; "prices go up more slowly. Usually not down".
pages.pictures: as before. Ends on works B: smoke thins, the lights dim, the queue returns: MORE WORKERS AT THE GATE.

pages.name: Who pays, here
pages.text: Who pays for the cure? From late twenty twenty-one into twenty twenty-three, the Reserve Bank raised its interest rate again and again. Many loans cost more, and jobs got harder to find. By the middle of twenty twenty-six... nearly six in a hundred were out of work. Up from about three. The interest rate isn't the only reason for that. So who pays for the cure? Many people with loans... and people put out of work.
terms_explained: who pays, said plainly at the end, so "pays" is heard as "who carries the harm", not "who hands over money for it". The share out of work is in the same unit as page 10, and the comparison is now said aloud.
pages.pictures: the dial climbs in steps: LATE 2021 TO 2023: AGAIN AND AGAIN (no rate figures). The 100-dot panel from page 10 returns with nearly 6 empty dots: NEARLY 6 IN 100 OUT OF WORK, Stats NZ, MIDDLE OF 2026, with a faint UP FROM ABOUT 3, and a small NOT THE ONLY REASON. Then WHO PAYS? lands over two cut-outs: MANY PEOPLE WITH LOANS / PEOPLE PUT OUT OF WORK.

pages.name: Two views
pages.text: America's version of our Reserve Bank has said the cure would probably mean fewer jobs. It sees that as unfortunate... but not the goal. Clara E. /məˈteɪi/ is the economist whose book this series follows. She argues that fewer jobs are the cure's main goal. With more workers waiting at the gate, she says, people with jobs have less power to ask for higher wages.
terms_explained: who Mattei is; the two views, now opposed on the same words ("fewer jobs... not the goal" against "fewer jobs are the cure's main goal"); "people with jobs"; "higher wages" (one name with page 10's wages).
pages.pictures: page-9 part B (code only): AMERICA'S VERSION OF OUR RESERVE BANK: FEWER JOBS: UNFORTUNATE, NOT THE GOAL (no quotation marks; small credit US FEDERAL RESERVE); her book with CLARA E. MATTEI, THE CAPITAL ORDER (2022); MATTEI ARGUES: FEWER JOBS ARE THE MAIN GOAL; the queue grows and the iron weight drops on the pay packet: LESS POWER TO ASK FOR HIGHER WAGES. No portrait.

pages.name: Back at the checkout
pages.text: And the checkout? Imagine the basket cost a hundred dollars in June twenty twenty-five. A year later, it cost about a hundred and four. If petrol and diesel prices hadn't changed... it would have cost about a hundred and three. When petrol and diesel go up, the price of almost everything made or moved goes up too... in both factories. So part of what you felt at the checkout came from petrol and diesel.
terms_explained: the two price figures, now in the page 1 basket's own unit (dollars), so no percent or decimal is needed; a second cause of prices going up, in plain words, working in both factories.
pages.pictures: a brief return to page-1's basket with a tag: $100, JUNE 2025; it flips to ABOUT $104, A YEAR LATER; a ghost tag beside it: ABOUT $103 IF PETROL AND DIESEL PRICES HADN'T CHANGED, credited STATS NZ (no 4.1%, 2.9% or 2026 on screen, since Malina doesn't say them on this page); the two-factories wide shot, the oil barrel lands by each works and both counters flip up: BOTH FACTORIES; back to the basket with PART OF IT: PETROL AND DIESEL.

pages.name: Spent on what?
pages.text: Does new money always push prices up? No. When new money is spent... and there are spare workers, materials and machines... it mostly gets more things made. When nothing is spare... it mostly pushes prices up. So next time you hear the warning... ask two questions. Spent on what... and is anything spare to make what it buys? And who pays for the cure?
